title: When the Mediterranean was a British lake
gist: Brendan Simms charts how Britain, between the 1620s and 1815, built a Mediterranean presence through Gibraltar, Menorca, Malta and the Ionian Islands, driven mainly by European balance-of-power strategy rather than trade. He opens with a 2026 drone strike on RAF Akrotiri during the second US-Iran war and HMS Dragon's slow response, an episode widely seen as a symbol of British decline.

insights.claim: Earlier in 2026, shortly after the second US-Iran war erupted, Britain's Sovereign Base Area at Akrotiri on Cyprus was struck by a drone believed launched from Lebanon, and HMS Dragon took so long to reach station that it became a national embarrassment.
insights.speaker: Brendan Simms
insights.so_what: Signals limited UK naval capacity and the vulnerability of Eastern Mediterranean bases in a Middle East war.
insights.locator: Earlier this year, shortly after the second US-Iran war

insights.claim: Simms predicts that the Akrotiri episode will not be the last British fiasco in the Mediterranean, setting it alongside Suez in 1956 and the loss of Menorca in 1756.
insights.speaker: Brendan Simms
insights.so_what: Expect continued questions over UK power projection and defence readiness.
insights.quote: This was not the first British fiasco in the Mediterranean, and it will not be the last.
insights.locator: This was not the first British fiasco

themes.theme: Bases as the foundation of seapower

insights.claim: Early English naval efforts against the Barbary Corsairs, such as Mansell's 1620-21 squadron and Blake's 1650s campaigns, were limited by the lack of a permanent local base.
insights.speaker: Brendan Simms
insights.so_what: Forward basing is the binding constraint on sustained naval power projection.

insights.claim: Tangier, acquired in Catherine of Braganza's dowry, enabled the 'Mediterranean Pass' protecting English shipping, but was abandoned in 1684 as unpopular and expensive to defend against Moroccan attacks.
insights.speaker: Brendan Simms
insights.so_what: Shows the cost-benefit trade-off of maintaining overseas bases.

insights.claim: Blake's 1654 blockade of the Straits of Gibraltar, preventing French fleets from Brest and Toulon from combining, was the first use of a stratagem central to later British naval strategy.
insights.speaker: Brendan Simms
insights.so_what: Chokepoint control is a recurring source of maritime leverage.

insights.claim: Under the 1713 Treaty of Utrecht Britain retained Gibraltar and Menorca, converting a transient naval presence into a permanent physical one with forts, garrison churches and port facilities.
insights.speaker: Brendan Simms
insights.so_what: Permanent infrastructure, not episodic deployment, defines a regional power.
insights.quote: This was now a permanent physical presence rather than a transient naval one.
insights.locator: At the Treaty of Utrecht in 1713

insights.claim: By 1815 Britain held Gibraltar, Malta and the Ionian Islands, transforming a sea where it had no base around 1700 into a 'British lake'.
insights.speaker: Brendan Simms
insights.so_what: Long-run illustration of how chokepoint and base networks underpin hegemony.
insights.locator: At the start of the 18th century

insights.claim: Simms argues Britain was in the Mediterranean partly for commerce such as the Levant trade and later the Suez Canal, but chiefly to uphold the European balance of power on which its security rested.
insights.speaker: Brendan Simms
insights.so_what: Geopolitical positioning in key seas is driven by security more than trade returns.
insights.locator: Britain was in the Mediterranean partly

insights.claim: Gibraltar and Menorca were treated as instruments and bargaining counters rather than ends in themselves; London repeatedly offered to return Gibraltar, but Spain's wider demands and British public opinion prevented it.
insights.speaker: Brendan Simms
insights.so_what: Territorial assets can become politically locked in once public opinion attaches to them.
insights.quote: Gibraltar and Menorca were instruments, not ends in themselves.
insights.locator: In this context, Gibraltar and Menorca

insights.claim: Napoleon's capture of Malta and landing in Egypt gave the Mediterranean two new roles in British thinking: propping up the ailing Ottoman Empire and protecting the route to India.
insights.speaker: Brendan Simms
insights.so_what: Shows how threats to trade routes to key markets reshape strategic priorities.
insights.locator: It was during the siege of Toulon

insights.claim: The Mediterranean was uniquely suited to seapower because littoral states were extremely vulnerable to a navy that could appear and vanish quickly; in 1742 Commodore Martin forced Naples out of an anti-Austrian coalition by threatening to level the royal palace.
insights.speaker: Brendan Simms
insights.so_what: Coastal economies and capitals remain exposed to naval coercion.

insights.claim: In 1718 Admiral Byng's squadron annihilated the Spanish fleet off Cape Passaro even though Britain and Spain were not formally at war, after Defoe warned that Spanish control of Sicily would choke British Levant commerce.
insights.speaker: Brendan Simms
insights.so_what: Precedent for pre-emptive naval action to protect sea lanes.

insights.claim: Britain's Mediterranean position came under intolerable pressure when it fought the American colonists, France, Spain and the Dutch at once; Gibraltar survived a siege of over three and a half years (1779-83) but Menorca was lost.
insights.speaker: Brendan Simms
insights.so_what: Multi-front conflict strains even dominant naval powers' ability to hold distant positions.
insights.locator: Britain did not have it all its own way.

insights.claim: France's 1768 annexation of Corsica showed the limits of British power, as London ultimately accepted there was nothing it could do.
insights.speaker: Brendan Simms
insights.so_what: Even hegemons tolerate adverse faits accomplis when costs are too high.
insights.locator: Britain did not have it all its own way.

insights.claim: Lord William Bentinck effectively ran Sicily and forced through an 1812 constitution abolishing feudalism; Lampedusa later regretted the British departure as Sicily's last chance to escape its dismal history.
insights.speaker: Brendan Simms
insights.so_what: External powers can catalyse institutional reform, though often transiently.
insights.locator: Britain’s presence on Sicily was brief

insights.claim: Many British wartime gains, including Sicily, Menorca and the Dalmatian islands, were given up after 1802 and 1815, but the Royal Navy came to dominate the region strategically and psychologically even where it lacked permanent bases.
insights.speaker: Brendan Simms
insights.so_what: Perceived dominance can outlast physical presence, shaping regional behaviour.
insights.quote: Strategically and psychologically, though, the Royal Navy now dominated the area, even where it had no permanent bases.
